new_statements.quote: Both tone (use of pitch variation in distinguishing words lexically or grammatically) and intonation (use of pitch variation mainly for expressing emotions and attitudes) feature in Ika. There are two major tones: high and low. The third, downstep, is not a major tone but a downstepped high. [...] Intonation is one of the major features in which Ika phonology differs from many Igbo dialects. Intonation involves the use of to express various meanings, for example attitudinal and emotional, and to mark syntactic form. Also, in the use of intonation, an utterance has only one prominent syllable (the nuclear syllable). These two features are observed in Ika but not in the Standard or other Igbo dialects.
new_statements.citation: Uguru, Joy Oluchi. 2015. Ika Igbo (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 45(2): 213-219. doi:10.1017/S0025100315000067
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ika is a two-tone language (H, L, plus downstep) in which every syllable bears a lexical tone; there is no word-level stress rule. Prominence exists only at the level of the intonation group: each utterance (intonation group) has a single prominent nuclear syllable that carries one of six intonation tunes. Uguru 2014 (abstract only) calls this nucleus 'a stressed syllable' and states that any other degrees of stress are subsumed under tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the 2015 Illustration; Uguru 2014 abstract: 'Other degrees of stress are subsumed under tone since every syllable bears a tone.'
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Tonal changes, losses and masking occur at nuclear syllables (Uguru 2014 abstract).
new_statements.domain_note: Utterance / intonation-group domain, not word. The 2015 Illustration is based on one 50-year-old female speaker (the author) reading isolated words and a passage. Supporting statement from Uguru 2014 abstract (OpenAIRE record saved): 'Hence in Ika, every intonation group (or tonal intonation group) has a nucleus (a stressed syllable) and it is this nucleus that bears the intonation. [...] Other degrees of stress are subsumed under tone since every syllable bears a tone.' Full paper not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Uguru 2015/2014 treat Ika as a dialect of Igbo ('Ika Igbo', West Niger / Niger Igbo cluster) spoken in Ika South and Ika North East LGAs (Delta State) and Igbanke (Edo State); this is the same variety as Glottolog ikaa1238 / ISO ikk. Speaker in the JIPA Illustration is the author (one female speaker); the Wikipedia article names Akumuzi, Owa and Agbor dialects but the sources do not specify which was recorded.

sources.note: No word 'stress' anywhere. p. 216 'Intonation system': two major tones H and L plus downstep; tone is lexically distinctive. p. 217: in the use of intonation 'an utterance has only one prominent syllable (the nuclear syllable)'; six intonation tunes carried by the nucleus. Prominence described only at utterance level.
